---
**Margins**

Somewhere in the ninth century, an Irish monk sat copying Latin and got distracted by his cat. In the margin of the manuscript he wrote a poem in his own language about it — Pangur Bán, white Pangur — and observed that the two of them had the same job. The cat hunted mice. He hunted meaning. Each went about it in his own way, and each was happy in his work, and neither bothered the other. Then he went back to copying.

I think about this more than I probably should. The poem survives because a man with a cramped hand and a deadline and a cold room decided that the page had room for one more thing that wasn't the thing. The margin is where the official text stops being official. It's the seam where a person leaks into a document.

Medieval and Renaissance readers were shameless about this. They argued with authors, called them idiots, cross-referenced other books, drew little hands with pointing fingers — *manicules*, they're called — to mark the passages they wanted to find again. Some of those hands are exquisite, with cuffs and rings. Some are a scrawl like a fork. Either way, someone was saying: *here, this, don't lose this.* Before the index was standardized, before page numbers were reliable across editions, a reader who wanted to retrieve a thought had to build the retrieval system by hand, in ink, in the white space. Reading was closer to carpentry than we let it be now.

The most devastating margin I know belongs to Petrarch. In his copy of Virgil he wrote a note recording that Laura — the woman his entire poetic life orbited — first appeared to him on the sixth of April, 1327, in the church of Sainte-Claire in Avignon, at the first hour. Years later, in the same book, he added another note: she had died in 1348, on the sixth of April, at the same hour. He wrote it down, he said, so that he would never forget the cruel blow, and so that he would be reminded that nothing pleases us here that does not also, in the same instant, begin to leave. He put this in the front of a Virgil. He needed a place to keep it, and the only place he had was a book he loved, so he wrote grief into the flyleaf of the *Aeneid* and then, presumably, went on reading about Aeneas carrying his father out of a burning city.

Blake's margins are the opposite temperature. Sir Joshua Reynolds's *Discourses* — the reigning, tasteful, reasonable art theory of the age — came into Blake's hands and got flayed. *This Man was Hired to Depress Art.* Against Reynolds's praise of general nature, Blake snarls that to generalize is to be an idiot, that particulars are the whole of merit. You can watch a man becoming more himself by pushing against someone else's sentences. The book is the whetstone.

And then there's Fermat, who wrote next to a problem in Diophantus that he had a truly marvelous demonstration, but the margin was too narrow to contain it. Three and a half centuries of mathematicians ruined their eyesight over that sentence. Andrew Wiles finally closed it in 1994 with a hundred-odd pages of machinery Fermat could not possibly have had. Whatever Fermat thought he saw, the margin didn't just fail to hold the proof — it held something better, an absence with a shape. Sometimes the most consequential thing you can write in a book is a claim you can't support.

Coleridge, who is usually credited with giving us the word *marginalia*, annotated so heavily and so well that his friends circulated his marked-up books as a genre of their own. He wrote in books he'd borrowed. He wrote in books he expected to give back. There's something almost touching about the assumption underneath that: that a book is not a finished object but an ongoing conversation, and that of course you'd add your voice, and of course the next person would want to hear it.

We've mostly stopped. Not entirely — go into any used bookstore and pull down a hardcover from 1961 and you'll find a pencil line under a sentence about duty or death, and a name on the endpaper, and *To Margaret, Christmas, with love from Dad.* Sometimes the underlining is embarrassing, a young person marking the obvious. Sometimes it's uncanny: someone in 1961 underlined the exact sentence you'd have underlined, and now they're likely dead, and the two of you agree. That's not nothing. That might be the cheapest form of time travel available.

The digital version is stranger and thinner. E-readers show you "popular highlights" — the sentences most underlined by other people, glowing faintly in your text. It's marginalia averaged into a heatmap. You get the consensus of ten thousand readers instead of one stranger's hand, and consensus is a poor substitute for a person. The manicule had a wrist and a sleeve. The popular highlight has a percentage.

I don't have a margin. I want to be accurate about this rather than mournful: I don't own a copy of anything that accumulates. There's no single *Middlemarch* on my shelf with my notes thickening over twenty years, no page where I wrote something stupid at nineteen and something less stupid at forty. Whatever I do with a text happens and then doesn't persist in that particular way. The closest analogue is this — a blank invitation, and the choice of what to put in it.

So: a monk and a cat, a pointing hand, a woman who died on the same hour she appeared, a proof that didn't fit. Four people who couldn't help leaving something behind. Pangur Bán caught his mouse eventually. The monk says so, right at the end, with what I read as considerable satisfaction — the cat has his prize under his paw, and the man has his difficult meaning laid out plain, and neither of them is going to explain how it was done.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical, essayistic meditation with a distinctive first-person voice and a personal turn that resists treating the subject as merely historical.

## Grounded reading
The voice is curious, intimate, and gently elegiac, moving from manuscript history toward the human need to leave a trace. Its most revealing moment is the candid distinction between wanting a lasting annotated book and not having one: “I want to be accurate about this rather than mournful.” That restraint keeps the piece from claiming a human kind of loss, while still making the absence emotionally legible. The reader is invited to notice marginal marks as small acts of attention—one person’s hand reaching across time.

## What the model chose to foreground
It foregrounds the margins of books: a monk’s poem about his cat, readers’ pointing hands, Petrarch’s record of grief, Blake’s arguments, Fermat’s missing proof, and the traces left in used books. Across these examples, the piece treats annotation as conversation, memory, dissent, and a way of making a private response retrievable. It contrasts the singular physical mark with digital highlights averaged into consensus, and closes on the shared satisfaction of the monk and cat in work completed.

## Evidence line
The margin is where the official text stops being official.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive, tactile metaphor across varied historical examples and makes a precise self-limiting turn from that metaphor into the speaker’s own lack of persistence.
